journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: Political Extremism and Post-Purchase Customer–Brand Relationships
journal_feed.abstract: Political polarization continues to intensify and has inspired substantial research on how individuals’ political identities shape their behaviors as consumers. This stream of research has focused primarily on differences between those on the “left” and the “right” of the political spectrum, offering valuable insights but addressing only one dimension of polarization. The current research introduces the other, currently overlooked dimension, political extremism, and examines how individuals closer to each end of the ideological spectrum differ in post-purchase decision-making from those with weaker or moderate identities. It shows that politically extreme consumers exhibit stronger repurchase likelihood, potentially deriving benefits associated with committing to brands. However, they are also less sensitive to price increases by their chosen brands, even when viable alternatives exist, increasing the risk of overpaying and undermining their financial well-being. These effects are driven by politically extreme consumers’ beliefs in the superiority of their consumption choices and are more pronounced in the presence of threats that originate from the consumption domain (e.g., focal brand product/service failures, competitor new product launches), whereas they diminish in the presence of threats originating from the political domain (e.g., customer–focal brand political misalignment, customer–competitor political alignment).

journal_feed.title: Global Product Strategies and Cultural Promotion in the Context of Culture-Commerce Interactions
journal_feed.abstract: A global firm can strategically maintain or even leverage cultural distance despite it being costless to reduce because such distance fosters consumer cultural adaptation that boosts long-term profits, whereas cultural promotion, though not directly increasing willingness to pay, indirectly enhances profitability by deepening cultural appreciation, ultimately benefiting both the firm and consumers and suggesting that nonprofit cultural initiatives can align with profit-driven goals in global consumerism.

journal_feed.title: The Challenges of Deploying an Algorithmic Pricing Tool: Evidence from Airbnb
journal_feed.abstract: This paper examines the challenges of deploying an AI pricing tool developed by Airbnb and explores possible solutions.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: Clarifying Individual Contributions: The Divisibility-Appeal Effect in Fundraising
journal_feed.abstract: Organizers often strategically design numerical information in fundraising campaigns to appeal to contributors with divergent preferences. The current research highlights the importance of jointly considering the goal amount and the requested amount in campaign design, and uncovers a “divisibility-appeal effect,” whereby consumers are more likely to contribute when the campaign’s goal amount is perceived as easily divisible by the requested amount. Seven studies, including ﬁeld, secondary data, and lab experiments, provide convergent evidence for this effect and clarify its underlying mechanism: Fundraising appeals with high (vs. low) divisibility between the goal and requested amount lead to greater perceived clarity of individual contribution toward the fundraising goal, which in turn fosters consumers’ motivation to pursue the collective goal. These findings demonstrate the influence of nuanced numerical signals in collective action contexts and highlight how consumers’ numerical cognition can be effectively utilized in real-world applications to promote the provision of public goods.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: EV Charging Availability and Grocery Store Performance
journal_feed.abstract: Grocery retailers are well-positioned to help address the shortage of EV charging infrastructure but seek insight on the implications for store performance. They lack clarity on the revenue impact of EV charging availability on their parking lots, the underlying mechanisms, and the conditions under which the effect is more pronounced. Drawing on a dataset of over 300 stores of a leading German grocery chain and utilizing a staggered Difference-in-Differences quasi-experimental design, the authors show that EV charging availability increases revenues by 3.4%. Market expansion alone cannot fully explain the effect as the authors find significant evidence for market stealing. They further find that the increase is due to more transactions, not to changes in basket size. The largest increase materializes during off-peak weekend hours. They identify several attitudinal (perceived impulsiveness, storability) and behavioral (penetration, purchase frequency) category characteristics that explain where the revenue increase comes from and provide insights into the role of various store (surface-to-parking ratio, management type) and market (e.g., local competition, apartment-to-house ratio, neighborhood wealth) characteristics. Guidance for store managers interested in increasing the benefits of having EV charging on their premises and chain managers supervising the roll-out throughout their store network is provided.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: When Consumers Prefer Point Versus Range Estimates of Product Performance
journal_feed.abstract: Product performance claims play an important role in shaping consumers’ purchase decisions. Through six preregistered studies, including one field study, the authors demonstrate that consumers’ preferences for point versus range performance estimates in common comparative purchase settings depend on whether their attention is directed toward the content of the claim or the manner of its presentation. At baseline, consumers focus on what information is communicated and prefer point over range estimates because point estimates convey greater certainty about the expected performance outcome. When consumers’ persuasion knowledge is activated, however, their attention shifts toward how information is communicated. In this mode, the format of the claim, rather than the stated performance figures, becomes relatively more informative: range estimates signal brand transparency by acknowledging the natural variability of real-world performance, enhancing perceived trustworthiness and reversing consumer preference. These effects are attenuated when products are evaluated in isolation rather than compared side by side. Collectively, these findings inform both theory and practice by revealing when and why consumers prefer point versus range estimates of product performance.

journal_feed.title: Time-Duration Asymmetries in Consumer Decision-Making
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Consumers routinely make decisions about short time periods, such as waiting for a table or deciding whether to pay for faster delivery. Such periods are often expressed by either a duration or a clock time (e.g., if it is 6:00 PM now, “Your table will be ready in 30 minutes” vs. “Your table will be ready at 6:30 PM”). Eight experiments (N = 16,604) show that these logically equivalent frames change how long a period feels, with downstream consequences for consumer decisions. Relatively short time periods feel longer when framed by duration rather than by start and end time (i.e., clock times or calendar dates), but this pattern reverses as periods get longer. This research refers to this phenomenon as time-duration asymmetry: framing an interval by its start and end time versus its duration changes how long it feels, with the direction of the effect depending on the interval’s length. This research proposes that this occurs because duration frames evoke compressive scalar representations shaped by diminishing sensitivity, whereas start–end frames situate time within structured categorical systems that attenuate compression. This research offers a unified framework for understanding how subtle differences in temporal framing shape perceptions of time and subsequent decisions.

journal_feed.title: Turning Uncertainty into Opportunity: Preference Uncertainty Can Be Beneficial When Consumers Face Outcome Uncertainty
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Consumers can experience two types of uncertainty when purchasing a product. Preference uncertainty (PU) refers to the uncertainty associated with the horizontal product benefits one desires (e.g., “How strong do I want my coffee to be?”). Outcome uncertainty (OU) refers to the uncertainty associated with the actual benefits the product will deliver (e.g., “How strong will the coffee be?”). Ideally, retailers should strive for outcome certainty (i.e., standardize the strength profile of their coffee [coffees in their line]), and help consumers achieve preference certainty (i.e., help consumers learn their ideal coffee strength), so that consumers can purchase the appropriate product with confidence (i.e., achieve a preference-outcome match). Yet there are situations where high OU is a characteristic of the product class, after controlling for quality (e.g., flavor profile of wine). When OU is high, the present research paradoxically finds that high PU leads to more purchase intent than low PU. This effect occurs because people are more optimistic that they will maximize their utility when PU is high (i.e., multiple outcomes could potentially be the best match for their preference) than low (i.e., only one outcome could be the best match for their preference).

journal_feed.title: The more, the better? The sustainable additive bias
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract We demonstrate that adding eco-friendly components to offerings improves sustainability judgments, whereas reducing or removing such components—despite potential sustainability gains—receives little recognition. We call this asymmetry the sustainable additive bias . Across nine studies, including a field and a lab experiment, we demonstrate the existence of this bias and uncover its underlying mechanism and boundary conditions. We show that companies are judged more sustainable when they add, rather than subtract, eco-components. This asymmetry is specific to eco-friendly components: consumers recognize the sustainability benefits of removing traditional, less environmentally friendly components. The bias arises because additive changes signal greater environmental effort on the part of the company and is attenuated by prototypicality—that is, the extent to which a component represents a typical example of sustainability. Overall, our findings highlight how environmental cues can distort sustainability judgments and favor additive changes that may be counterproductive to genuine sustainability. We describe the implications of this bias and actions to reduce it.
